introduction-the-integrity-problem.core: To check that two copies of a large dataset are identical, or that a downloaded file hasn't been tampered with, comparing every byte is too expensive across a network. A hash gives a short fingerprint, but a single hash tells you only that something differs, not where. Merkle trees hash in a hierarchy so you can both verify and locate differences cheaply.

first_principles.problem: Two replicas of a 1 TB table disagree, and comparing them row-by-row over the network would take hours.
truths: One hash can't locate a difference.

analogy.title: Checking a library by shelf totals
analogy.story: Compare each floor's book count first, then the shelves on the floor that differs, then the books on that shelf.
analogy.breaks: Counts can match by coincidence; good hashes almost never collide.

example.title: Replica check
flow: Merkle: compare root, then children, ~log2(n) levels

check.q: Why isn't a single hash of the whole dataset enough for repair?
check.a: It tells you the copies differ but not which part differs, so you'd still have to compare everything.

anatomy-of-a-merkle-tree.core: Split data into blocks and hash each one: those are the leaves. Each parent node is the hash of its children's hashes concatenated, up to a single root hash that commits to all the data. Change one byte anywhere and the leaf, every ancestor and the root all change; the tree height is log2 of the number of blocks.

first_principles.problem: An engineer stores only per-block hashes and can't cheaply prove the whole set is consistent.
derivation: Use **domain separation** for leaf vs node.

analogy.title: A family tree of signatures
analogy.story: Each parent signs a page listing their children's signatures, so forging any descendant changes the founder's signature.
analogy.breaks: Signatures need keys; hashes need none, just collision resistance.

example.title: Building a root
example.outcome: a root committing to every block.

check.q: Why prefix leaves and internal nodes differently?
check.a: Domain separation stops an attacker presenting an internal node as a leaf to forge a proof (second-preimage attack).

efficient-verification-merkle-proofs.core: To prove a block belongs to a dataset with a known root, you don't send the whole dataset, just the block plus the sibling hash at each level up to the root (the audit path). The verifier rehashes upward and checks the result equals the trusted root. Proof size and work are O(log n): about 20 hashes for a million blocks.

first_principles.problem: A light client wants to confirm one transaction is in a block without downloading every transaction.
truths: Siblings let you recompute the path.
derivation: Trust the root via **signature or consensus**.

analogy.title: Proving you're in a family photo album
analogy.story: Instead of the whole album, you show your photo plus the label on each folder up to the album's sealed cover.
analogy.breaks: Labels can be copied; hashes can't be forged without breaking the hash function.

example.title: Verify a proof
example.outcome: membership proven in a few hundred bytes.

check.q: How many hashes are in a proof for 1,048,576 leaves?
check.a: 20, one sibling per level, since log2(1,048,576) = 20.

anti-entropy-finding-the-difference-betw.core: Eventually consistent databases (Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak) use Merkle trees for anti-entropy repair. Each replica builds a tree over its key range; replicas exchange roots and walk down only the subtrees whose hashes differ, then stream just the mismatched key ranges. This keeps repair traffic proportional to the differences, not the data size.

first_principles.problem: Full repair streams the entire dataset between replicas weekly, saturating the network.
truths: Replicas drift due to missed writes.

analogy.title: Two accountants reconciling ledgers
analogy.story: They compare yearly totals, then monthly, then daily, and only pull receipts for days that don't match.
analogy.breaks: Ledgers are static; replicas change during repair, so trees are snapshots.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only 3 ranges streamed, not the whole table.

code.text:
nodetool repair -pr keyspace1          # primary range, Merkle-based
nodetool repair --full keyspace1       # rebuild trees from scratch
# logs: 'Endpoints /10.0.0.2 and /10.0.0.3 have 3 range(s) out of sync'

check.q: Why must Cassandra repair run within gc_grace_seconds?
check.a: Otherwise tombstones may be purged before reaching all replicas, and repair would resurrect deleted data.

immutable-ledgers-blockchains.core: Blockchains, Git and Certificate Transparency logs chain hashes so history is tamper-evident: each block or commit contains the hash of its predecessor and a Merkle root of its contents. Altering anything in the past changes every later hash, so anyone holding a recent hash can detect rewriting. Tamper-evident is not tamper-proof; consensus or audit decides which history is accepted.

first_principles.problem: An auditor needs assurance that past log entries weren't silently edited.
truths: Changing the past changes the head.

analogy.title: A notary book with numbered, sealed pages
analogy.story: Each page quotes the seal of the previous one, so ripping out or rewriting a page breaks every seal after it.
analogy.breaks: A forger could rewrite every page; detection needs others to hold old seals.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Anyone with the old HEAD hash sees history was rewritten.

code.text:
git cat-file -p HEAD
# tree 9c1f...      <- Merkle root of files
# parent 4ab2...    <- previous commit hash
# author ...
git rebase -i HEAD~3   # rewriting changes every later hash

check.q: Why is a hash chain tamper-evident but not tamper-proof?
check.a: Someone can rewrite and rehash everything; it's only detected if others hold the earlier hashes to compare against.
